common_name: St. Brigid Anemone (Semi-Double Florist Poppy Anemone)

planting.note: Soak corms in room-temperature water for a few hours before planting 2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens, plant corms in October or November for winter-to-spring bloom, since temperatures above 75°F send plants into dormancy.

directions: Soak corms briefly before planting 2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. St. Brigid is the classic semi-double counterpart to the single-flowered De Caen anemone, producing fuller, more ruffled 2-3 inch poppy-like blooms in a similarly brilliant range of colors — crimson, scarlet, violet, pink, and white — all centered with dramatic black stamens. Like De Caen, it is a favorite cut flower for the cool-season garden, lasting well in a vase, and performs best where winters are mild enough for fall planting and a winter-to-spring bloom season, going dormant once summer heat arrives. Corms are inexpensive and effective planted in generous masses for a spectacular display, and in regions too cold for fall planting, corms can be started indoors in late winter for spring bloom instead.

common_name: The Giant Colchicum (Large Pale Lilac-Pink Autumn Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer to early fall, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; corms often begin flowering within days of planting, even before they are in the ground.

directions: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. The Giant is one of the largest and most vigorous colchicum hybrids, sending up goblet-shaped, pale lilac-pink flowers with a white throat directly from the ground in early fall, appearing before any foliage emerges, which is followed the next spring by large, glossy, strap-like leaves that die back by early summer and must be left to yellow naturally to recharge the corm. Its unusual bloom sequence — flowers with no leaves in fall, leaves with no flowers in spring — surprises gardeners unfamiliar with the genus, so mark planting locations to avoid accidental disturbance. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas grazed by pets or livestock, and its large spring foliage needs room among companion plants that will not be smothered.

common_name: Lilac Wonder Colchicum (Early Rosy-Lilac Autumn Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer to early fall, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Lilac Wonder is one of the earliest colchicum cultivars to bloom, often flowering in late summer before most others.

directions: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Lilac Wonder produces goblet-shaped, rosy-lilac flowers with a white basal blush, blooming leafless directly from bare ground earlier in the season than many colchicum cultivars, often as early as late summer, and reliably multiplying into generous clumps over the years. The following spring brings large, glossy, strap-shaped leaves with no flowers, which must be left to die back naturally by early summer to recharge the corm for the next autumn's bloom. Its compact size compared to some larger colchicum hybrids makes it a good choice for smaller naturalized plantings or rock gardens. All parts are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from areas where pets or livestock might graze.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Caerulea bears semi-double, sky-blue flowers rather than the single flowers of the species, on tall spikes well suited to a moist meadow or border planting.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; camassia tolerates seasonally wet spring soil better than most bulbs but appreciates drier conditions during its summer dormancy. Caerulea bears tall, upright spikes of semi-double, clear sky-blue, star-shaped flowers in late spring, fuller and showier than the single flowers of the wild species, rising well above strappy, grass-like foliage. Native in form to wet meadows of the Pacific Northwest, it naturalizes readily in a moist border or meadow planting and combines beautifully with late tulips and ornamental grasses. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to recharge the bulb, and established clumps need little care beyond occasional division if flowering declines after many years.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Sacajawea combines creamy-white flowers with cream-margined variegated foliage, giving two seasons of ornamental interest.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; camassia tolerates seasonally wet spring soil better than most bulbs but prefers drier conditions during summer dormancy. Sacajawea pairs creamy-white, star-shaped flowers on tall spring spikes with strappy foliage edged in a crisp white-cream variegation, giving the plant ornamental value both in and out of bloom, unlike the plain green foliage of most camassia selections. Native in form to wet meadows of the Pacific Northwest, it naturalizes well in a moist border or meadow setting and pairs nicely with blue-flowered camassia cultivars or late tulips for contrast. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to recharge the bulb for next year, and established clumps need minimal care beyond occasional division after many years if flowering declines.
